props.title: Baby Face

sections.content: Baby Face (1933) stands as one of Pre-Code Hollywood's most daring films, following Barbara Stanwyck's Lily Powers as she sleeps her way to the top of a New York bank. The film's raw portrayal of sexual manipulation shocked audiences, leading to significant censorship cuts. Director Alfred E. Green and Stanwyck created a provocative critique of capitalism and gender politics that feels radical even today. This fits alongside other boundary-pushing Pre-Code films like Red-Headed Woman (1932) and The Divorcee (1930) that depicted women's sexuality with unprecedented frankness before the Production Code clamped down in 1934.

sections.content: The Pre-Code era (1929-1934) represented Hollywood's most experimental period regarding adult themes. Films like Three on a Match (1932) tackled drug addiction, while Safe in Hell (1931) dealt with prostitution and murder. Baby Face pushed boundaries furthest with its Nietzschean philosophy explicitly advocating using sex for power. The original uncut version, rediscovered in 2004, includes scenes and dialogue deemed too shocking in 1933, like direct references to Lily's prostitution and more overt sexuality.

Stanwyck's performance as Lily Powers defined the Pre-Code archetype of the unrepentant "bad girl" who refuses to be punished for her sexuality. Unlike later femme fatales, Lily's motivations stem from poverty and abuse rather than pure malice. The film's critique of predatory male behavior and corporate exploitation remains startlingly relevant, influencing later films like The Apartment (1960) and Working Girl (1988). sections.content: The enforcement of the Production Code effectively banned films like Baby Face for decades. Its frank treatment of female sexuality wouldn't be matched until the 1960s. Modern films like The Last Seduction (1994) and Atomic Blonde (2017) echo its themes of women weaponizing sexuality against patriarchal power structures, though few match its pre-Code boldness. The film's exploration of class mobility through sexual manipulation influenced everything from Double Indemnity (1944) to Body Heat (1981).
